title: ASCII Format for Network Interchange
summary: Specifies using the standard seven-bit ASCII character code for exchanging text between computers on the ARPANET, over host-to-host connections. It reproduces the USA Standard Code for Information Interchange and notes that each host defines its own break characters. It later became an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: Computers need to agree on which number means which letter. This note says everyone should use the same code table so a message typed on one computer reads the same on another.

questions: how is ascii encoded in a byte
subtitle: The early decision to exchange text over the ARPANET using seven-bit ASCII inside eight-bit bytes.

tldr.problem: Computers on the network needed to agree on which number stands for which character so that text typed on one host reads the same on another.
tldr.mechanism: The memo suggests standard 7-bit ASCII embedded in an 8-bit byte whose high-order bit is always 0, used over HOST-HOST primary connections, and reproduces the code table from USAS X3.4-1968.
tldr.outcome: Each host defines its own break characters, for example SRI uses a period and UCLA uses carriage return. The status is Internet Standard.

facts.label: Code width
facts.value: 7 bits, in an 8-bit byte with the high-order bit 0

today: RFC 20 is marked as an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Network Suggestion
sections.content:
The cover note suggests, for concreteness, the use of standard 7-bit ASCII embedded in an 8-bit byte whose high-order bit is always 0. The code is the one on the attached pages, copied from USAS X3.4-1968, and it is to be used over HOST-HOST primary connections.

Break characters are defined by the receiving remote host. The note gives two examples: SRI uses . (X'2E', or 2/14) as its end-of-line character, while UCLA uses X'0D', or 0/13, which is carriage return.
sections.eli5: Everyone puts the same seven-bit letter code into a box of eight, and leaves the extra bit empty. Each computer decides for itself what marks the end of a line.

sections.title: The Code Table and Positions
sections.content:
The standard code is drawn as a table with columns 0 to 7 and rows 0 to 15. The column number is the decimal value of bits b7, b6 and b5 taken together, and the row number is the decimal value of bits b4, b3, b2 and b1, where b7 is the high-order bit and b1 the low-order bit.

As an example, the character K sits in column 4, row 11, written 4/11, and its bits are 1 0 0 1 0 1 1. The code may be called ASCII or USASCII, and a year can be appended to name an earlier issue, as in "ASCII 63".
sections.eli5: The table is like a grid on a map. Each letter has a column and a row, and those two numbers are its secret code.

sections.title: Control and Graphic Characters
sections.content:
The legend splits the code into control characters and graphic characters. Control characters are marked as communication control (CC), format effector (FE) or information separator (IS). Examples are ACK and EOT for communication control, LF and CR for layout, and FS, GS, RS and US for separating information.

The four information separators are used in a hierarchy: FS is the most inclusive, then GS, then RS, and US is the least inclusive. DEL is listed with the controls but is not a control character in the strict sense. Some graphics, such as @, [ and {, should not be used in international interchange without agreement between sender and recipient.
sections.eli5: Some codes are letters you can see. Others are signals like ring the bell, start a new line, or stop here.

sections.title: Scope and General Considerations
sections.content:
The standard says it does not define how the code is recorded on any physical medium, and it has no redundancy or error control. It also does not define character structure for data communication, formats, code extension or how control characters are drawn.

Deviations from the standard may create serious difficulties and should be used only with full cognizance of the parties involved. Collation order is defined by the binary values of the characters, and no meaning is prescribed for the graphics beyond what users understand.
sections.eli5: The code only says which number is which letter. It does not say how to store it or check for mistakes, and it asks everyone to follow the table closely.
